0.label: A player captures an apparently free or high-value piece while fatally neglecting an immediate threat left behind by that very move.
0.description: In every position, the blundering player spots a material gain — a hanging piece, pawn, queen, or exchange — and executes the capture without checking what their own move enables or uncovers for the opponent. The act of capturing either vacates a critical defensive square, opens a file or diagonal, or removes a key defender, allowing an immediate checkmate or decisive tactical blow. The unifying pattern is the tunnel-vision capture: the player sees what they are taking but not what they are giving away by moving that piece.

1.label: Activating a rook to a 'natural' file wastes the one critical tempo needed to address an urgent tactical or positional threat.
1.description: In every position, a player moves a dormant rook to what appears to be a logical, active square (open file, central file, battery setup) while completely ignoring an immediate crisis — a hanging piece, an uncastled king, a tactical shot, or a positional weakness that demanded attention right now. The rook development is not wrong in principle, but the timing is catastrophically bad because the opponent's best response exploits exactly what the rook move failed to address. The unifying coaching lesson is: before activating a rook 'by routine,' verify there is no forcing threat that makes the position's most urgent demand take absolute priority.

2.label: Castling moves that walk the king into immediate tactical refutations the player failed to calculate.
2.description: In every position, the player chose to castle (kingside or queenside) following general principles of king safety and rook activation, but the specific castled king position created or exposed a concrete tactical vulnerability — forks, hanging pieces, open diagonals, or tempo-gaining attacks — that the opponent could immediately exploit. The blunder is not that castling is inherently wrong, but that the player applied a strategic heuristic without calculating the forcing tactical consequences that castling triggered in that specific position.

3.label: A queen relocation that abandons a critical defensive or offensive duty, immediately exploited by the opponent.
3.description: In every position, the blundering side moves their queen to a seemingly active or logical square, but in doing so vacates a square or diagonal that was providing essential coverage — leaving a piece hanging, a key square undefended, or a tactical shot available that didn't exist before. The queen's new position offers little or no compensation for the defensive hole created, and the opponent can immediately exploit the newly undefended target with a forcing move. This is the classic pattern of 'the queen can only be in one place at a time' — overestimating the queen's activity on its new square while ignoring what it just stopped doing.

4.label: Moving the queen to an apparently active or safe square that immediately creates a decisive tactical vulnerability.
4.description: In every position, the player voluntarily relocates their queen to what seems like a centralizing or consolidating square, but the new square either leaves a piece undefended, allows an immediate fork or tempo-gaining attack, or abandons a critical defensive duty. The queen's departure from its previous square or arrival on the new square creates a concrete tactical refutation — often a knight fork, a hanging piece, or a passed pawn push — that wins material or delivers a decisive advantage. The unifying coaching lesson is that queen moves must be checked not just for what the queen gains, but for what it stops defending and what enemy tactics the new square enables.

5.label: A pawn advance on the flank creates or exposes a decisive tactical or structural weakness that is immediately exploited.
5.description: In every position, the blundering player pushed a pawn (g4, g5, g6, f3, f6, b4, c6) that either opened lines toward their own king, abandoned defense of a key piece, or created a permanent weakness that the opponent immediately exploited. The common pattern is not simply 'bad kingside pawn move' but rather a pawn advance that the player believed was proactive or safe, but which either removed a critical defender, created a new tactical target, or invited an immediate tactical refutation. The feature appears to detect the moment when a seemingly plausible flank or structural pawn push fatally compromises the position by ignoring an existing threat or creating a new one.

6.label: A pawn move played with a secondary goal (prophylaxis, space, safety) that wastes the only tempo needed to address an immediate tactical or positional crisis.
6.description: In every position, the player makes a pawn push (on the a-, b-, g-, or h-file) that pursues a plausible-looking secondary objective—advancing space, preventing an intrusion, or shoring up a weakness—while completely ignoring a concrete, forcing threat that the opponent can execute immediately afterward. The pawn move is irreversible and costs exactly one tempo, which is the one tempo the opponent needed to launch a decisive combination, capture a hanging piece, or deliver checkmate. The unifying coaching lesson is that before committing to any pawn move, the player must first verify whether the opponent has an immediate forcing reply that the position cannot survive.

7.label: Delivering a check that allows the king to escape to safety, wasting tempo and squandering a winning advantage.
7.description: In every position, the player reflexively plays a check expecting the opponent's king to be driven into danger or forced into perpetual harassment, but the king simply steps to a safe square, neutralizing all threats. The checking piece gains nothing — no material, no structural improvement, no mating net — while the opponent consolidates and often counterattacks decisively. The unifying lesson is that a check is only valuable if the king has no good escape; an 'automatic' check that the king can safely ignore is worse than a quiet developing or winning move.

8.label: Playing a non-urgent flank pawn advance that ignores a critical tactical or positional threat requiring immediate attention.
8.description: In every position, the player pushes a flank pawn (a2-a4, a6-a5, b7-b5, h2-h4, etc.) as a slow strategic or space-gaining move while the opponent has an urgent unaddressed threat—tactical, structural, or king-safety related—that punishes the wasted tempo immediately. The common coaching lesson is that flank pawn advances are 'quiet' moves that forfeit the initiative when the position demands concrete, forcing responses. The feature detects positions where a pawn push on the wing loses because it fails to address the most pressing requirement of the position.

9.label: A pawn move attacks or threatens an enemy piece but creates a larger tactical or structural weakness that the opponent immediately exploits.
9.description: In every position, the blundering side advances a pawn to attack or chase away an enemy piece (queen, knight, bishop), believing they are gaining a tempo or winning material. Instead, the pawn move either weakens the king's pawn shelter, vacates a critical square, removes a defender, or exposes the moving side's own pieces to a counter-tactic that outweighs whatever the pawn attack achieved. The opponent ignores or sidesteps the threat and punishes the structural or tactical concession created by the pawn advance itself.

10.label: A quiet king tuck or queen repositioning wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a forcing tactical response.
10.description: In every position, the player makes a seemingly sensible prophylactic or consolidating move (king to h1/h8, queen rerouting, rook centralizing) that does not address the immediate dynamic demands of the position. The opponent then exploits the gifted tempo with a forcing move — a pawn advance, piece leap, or tactical strike — that the blundering side had no time to meet. The unifying lesson is that in sharp or critical positions, quiet moves that ignore existing tension are punished immediately by tempo-gaining attacks.

11.label: Suboptimal king moves in late-stage king-and-pawn endgames where exact square choice is critical.
11.description: Every position involves a king move in a simplified endgame (mostly king-and-pawn or near-pawn endings) where the chosen square is either passive, retreating, or misaligned with the critical zone, allowing the opponent's king to seize key squares or establish opposition. The unifying pattern is that the side to move picks a plausible-looking king retreat or sidestep instead of the precise centralizing or aggressive king march that maintains or converts the advantage. This feature fires on king moves that represent a failure to calculate exact king geometry—opposition, outflanking, and pawn-race timing—in technical endgames.

12.label: Moving the queen away from a critical defensive post leaves the king or key squares fatally unguarded
12.description: In every position, the blundering player relocates their queen (or occasionally another piece) to an ambitious-looking but misguided square, physically removing it from the area where it was performing an essential defensive or tactical function. This abandonment immediately creates a concrete vulnerability—an undefended king, a loose piece, a back-rank weakness, or an unguarded diagonal—that the opponent exploits on the very next move. The unifying coaching lesson is that piece activity must be evaluated not just by where the piece is going, but by what critical duty it is abandoning.

13.label: Playing an aggressive or checking queen move that loses the initiative by giving the opponent a free developing or escaping tempo.
13.description: In every position, the player makes an impulsive queen move—often a check or apparent threat—that fails to maintain or convert an advantage because the opponent's forced response actually improves their position (king escapes danger, rook activates, piece develops, or a stronger threat is resolved for free). The common failure is prioritizing the appearance of aggression over concrete calculation: the move looks threatening but hands the opponent exactly the tempo they need. The feature detects queen moves that waste initiative by generating a 'threat' the opponent answers profitably, rather than finding the move that preserves or increases pressure.

14.label: A piece moves to a 'better' square but vacates a critical defensive duty, immediately creating a hanging piece or tactical weakness.
14.description: In every position, the blundering player makes a seemingly logical piece rerouting move — developing, repositioning, or activating a knight, bishop, or queen — without recognizing that the piece's departure removes the only or key defender of another piece or pawn. The opponent immediately exploits the newly undefended target with a capture, fork, or direct attack. The unifying coaching lesson is: before rerouting any piece, verify what it was defending on its current square.

15.label: Rook moves to an idle or wrong square, wasting tempo while the opponent advances a decisive threat.
15.description: In every position, the player moves their rook to a square that looks plausibly active (back rank, open file, seventh rank) but accomplishes nothing concrete, surrendering the initiative. The opponent immediately exploits the lost tempo to push a passed pawn, deliver check, or activate their own pieces decisively. The unifying pattern is not the specific tactic that follows, but the root cause: the rook relocation was a 'do-nothing' move in a position that demanded urgency.

16.label: A rook is repositioned for a plausible strategic reason while missing that the position demands an immediate tactical or defensive response.
16.description: In every case, the player moves a rook to a seemingly logical square — activating it, doubling on a file, defending a rank, or targeting a pawn — but fails to recognize that the position has a forcing, time-sensitive requirement (a mating threat, a fork, a check, or a critical pawn break) that the rook move does nothing to address or actively enables. The rook relocation wastes the one move available to handle the crisis, allowing the opponent to execute a tactic that was either already present or newly created by vacating the rook's original square. The unifying pattern is a plausible-looking rook maneuver that ignores the most urgent feature of the position.

17.label: A move that pursues a secondary plan while allowing the opponent to consolidate or counter-attack, wasting the initiative.
17.description: In every position, the player makes a plausible-looking move (developing a piece, advancing a pawn, repositioning a queen) that fails to press an existing advantage or address the most urgent threat, giving the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the position or seize the initiative. The common thread is not a specific tactical motif but a positional failure mode: the played move is too slow or misdirected relative to what the position demands, allowing the opponent to respond with a single strong move that either defends everything or creates an immediate decisive counter. The feature appears to detect positions where a player 'changes the subject' — pursuing their own plan while ignoring that the opponent now gets to solve all their problems in one move.

18.label: Moving a bishop to a seemingly better square while ignoring an immediate tactical or mating threat.
18.description: In every position, the player moves their bishop to a more 'active' or 'centralized' square as a positional improvement, but this bishop move is a quiet non-forcing move that consumes a critical tempo. The opponent then exploits that wasted move to deliver a decisive blow — whether a checkmate threat, a fork, a piece capture, or an unstoppable pawn advance — that the bishop move either enabled or failed to prevent. The unifying coaching lesson is: before repositioning a piece for positional reasons, always check whether the position demands an immediate forcing response.

19.label: Detects queen moves that reposition to an apparently active or logical square while fatally abandoning a critical defensive duty.
19.description: In every position, the player moves their queen to what seems like a reasonable or even strong square — centralizing, activating, or defending elsewhere — but the relocation removes the queen from a square where it was the sole or critical defender of the king or a key piece. The refutation in each case immediately exploits the newly unguarded target: a back rank, a mating square, a hanging piece, or a fork, that the queen's presence had been preventing. The unifying lesson is that queen moves must account for what defensive responsibilities are being abandoned, not just what threats are being created.

20.label: A king relocation move that walks away from a defended piece, leaving it suddenly unprotected and immediately capturable.
20.description: In every position, the blundering side makes a seemingly logical king move (centralizing, seeking safety, escaping threats, or tucking into a corner) that removes the king from a square where it was the sole defender of a piece or pawn. The opponent immediately exploits this by capturing the now-hanging material. The feature detects the pattern where a king move is the specific cause of creating an undefended piece rather than any other type of move.

21.label: A king move that appears safe or purposeful but immediately creates new tactical or strategic vulnerabilities.
21.description: In every position, the player moves their king with an ostensibly reasonable goal — safety, centralization, prophylaxis, or support — but the king's new square either abandons a critical defensive duty, steps into a fork or mating pattern, gifts a decisive tempo to the opponent, or removes the king from its optimal defensive post. The unifying thread is not a specific tactical motif but the meta-pattern: the king move itself is the blunder, transforming a tenable or even winning position into a lost one by misplacing the most important piece on the board.

22.label: A bishop development or repositioning move that ignores or enables an immediate tactical refutation already present in the position.
22.description: In every case, the player moves a bishop — whether developing it, unpinning, or repositioning — while failing to account for a concrete tactical threat that either already exists or is created by the bishop's departure from its current square. The bishop move looks natural or purposeful in isolation (development, castling prep, attack), but it either abandons a defensive duty, walks into a counter-tempo, or allows the opponent to execute a fork, pin, or king attack that was previously impossible. The feature fires on bishop moves where the positional justification is sound but the tactical consequence is immediately decisive.

23.label: Playing a cautious waiting or preventive move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a decisive counter.
23.description: In every position, the player makes a seemingly safe prophylactic or preparatory move (h3, h6, a3, a6, b6, f5) to prevent a perceived threat or gain minor positional benefit, but the move fails to address an immediate tactical or strategic opportunity the opponent has. The wasted tempo allows the opponent to immediately exploit a hanging piece, open the center, activate a piece, or seize a key square before the player can consolidate. The unifying coaching lesson is that prophylactic thinking must be subordinated to urgency: when the position demands concrete action, a passive waiting move can transform a good or equal position into a losing one in a single move.

24.label: Actively developing a bishop to an apparently aggressive square that turns out to be tactically or positionally unsound.
24.description: In every position, a player moves a bishop from its starting square (or repositions it) to what looks like an active, aggressive diagonal — typically c1→g5, c1→f4, c8→g4, f1→c4, f8→b4, etc. — without first verifying that the destination square is safe or that the bishop won't be immediately attacked, captured, or exploited. The unifying theme is premature or careless bishop development/redeployment where the bishop move either hangs the piece, loses tempo to a forcing response, or abandons a critical defensive duty, resulting in a large material or positional loss.

25.label: Moving a knight to a new square that is immediately hanging or critically weakens coordination
25.description: In every position, the player makes a knight move intended to reposition or improve the piece — whether developing, centralizing, rerouting, or retreating — but the destination square is either undefended (allowing immediate capture) or the knight's departure fatally loosens the position. The unifying error is not tactical blindness to a specific pattern but rather misjudging the safety or timing of a knight maneuver: the knight lands on a square where it can be taken for free, or leaves behind a critical defensive or offensive duty. This feature fires specifically on knight moves that appear purposeful and positionally motivated yet immediately lose material or decisive positional value.

26.label: Premature queen development that loses tempo and allows the opponent to gain initiative through counter-attacks.
26.description: In every position, the player moves their queen to an ostensibly active square early in the game or middlegame, but the queen immediately becomes a target for enemy pieces developing with tempo. The opponent responds by attacking the misplaced queen or exploiting the lack of coordination it creates, forcing the queen to retreat or losing material. This pattern captures the classic coaching principle that early queen sorties invite tempo-gaining counter-attacks that negate any initiative the move was meant to create.

27.label: Castling when an immediate tactical or material threat already exists in the position that castling fails to address.
27.description: In every position, the player castles (kingside or queenside) as a routine developing move to achieve king safety and connect rooks, but the position already contains an unresolved threat—a hanging piece, a tactical fork, a pin, or a tempo-gaining attack—that the opponent can exploit immediately after castling. The castling move wastes the turn needed to resolve the existing threat, allowing the opponent to cash in on it before the castled position provides any benefit. The unifying coaching lesson is: before castling, always verify there is no immediate tactical problem that your opponent can exploit on their very next move.

28.label: Castling that immediately exposes the king to tactical or structural attack
28.description: In every position, the player castles (either kingside or queenside) as a routine developing move without recognizing that the specific pawn structure, piece placement, or opponent's tactical resources make that king destination immediately unsafe. The refutations consistently involve direct pawn storms, piece sacrifices on the castled king's shelter, or exploitation of newly undefended pawns exposed by the castling rook's movement. The unifying lesson is that castling must be evaluated not as a general principle but as a concrete move — the destination square must be safe given the specific position.

29.label: Captures a pawn that immediately grants the opponent a powerful free tempo or tactical shot in return.
29.description: In every position, the blundering side captures a pawn (or exchanges pawns) expecting to gain material or open lines, but the capture either removes a key defender, opens a diagonal/file toward the captor's king, or hands the opponent a piece that lands on a dominant square with tempo. The opponent's immediate recapture or tactical response wins back more than the captured pawn's value, often with check or a fork, leaving the blunderer worse off than before the capture.

30.label: Giving an ineffective check that allows the opponent's king to escape to a better square or enables a defensive interposition, wasting a tempo and surrendering the initiative.
30.description: In every position, the player delivers a check (or forcing move) that feels aggressive but fails because the opponent's king simply steps to a safe or even improved square, or a defensive piece interposes with gain of tempo. The attacker assumed the check would maintain or increase pressure, but instead the forcing move hands the initiative to the opponent and dissipates a winning or drawing advantage. The unifying lesson is that checks are only as good as the king's escape routes — a check that improves the opponent's position is worse than not checking at all.

31.label: A rook move to an ostensibly active square ignores a more urgent threat or concedes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative decisively.
31.description: In every position, the blundering side slides a rook to what appears to be an active or logical square (7th rank, open file, attacking post), but the move either abandons control of a key square, undefends a piece, or wastes the one tempo needed to handle an opponent's threat. The opponent then immediately exploits the conceded tempo or vacated square with a fork, discovered attack, check, or material win that the rook move failed to address.

32.label: A pawn advance removes its guard from a previously protected square or piece, leaving material or a key square suddenly undefended.
32.description: In every position, the blundering player pushed a pawn forward with an active or structural intent, but failed to account for the fact that the pawn's departure from its original square stripped protection from a piece, square, or pawn it was previously guarding. The opponent immediately exploits the newly undefended target — capturing a hanging piece, forking exposed units, or invading a vacated square — turning the position from equal or winning to losing in one move. The unifying coaching lesson is: before advancing any pawn, verify what that pawn is currently defending and whether losing that guard is safe.

33.label: A rook move that places the piece on a passive or reactive square, surrendering the initiative and allowing the opponent to seize a decisive tempo or breakthrough.
33.description: In every position, the blundering side moves a rook (or occasionally another piece) to a square that appears defensive or logical but is fundamentally passive — defending a pawn, occupying a file, or retreating — while the opponent immediately exploits the gifted tempo with an active counter: an passed pawn advance, king activation, or tactical strike. The unifying thread is not the tactical motif that follows, but the structural error of reactive piece placement: instead of playing actively (activating the king, advancing a passer, or creating threats), the player makes a 'do-nothing' rook move that cedes the initiative and allows the opponent to dictate play.

34.label: King moves away from a square or piece it was defending, leaving material or pawns immediately capturable.
34.description: In every position, the king move looks purposeful—centralizing, attacking a pawn, or seeking safety—but the king was the sole guardian of a nearby pawn or piece. The moment the king steps away, the opponent simply captures what was left undefended, with no tactical trick required. The pattern is pure geometry: the king's new square is always further from the defended target than the attacker's piece needs.

35.label: Pushing a pawn aggressively to attack or break open the position before the tactical and positional groundwork is laid.
35.description: In every case, a player advances a pawn one square hoping to crack open the opponent's structure, create a passed pawn, or generate attacking chances — but the move either loses the pawn for free, allows the opponent to ignore it and strike elsewhere, or vacates a square that triggers an immediate tactical refutation. The unifying error is committing a pawn thrust that the position cannot yet support: the break is premature because the supporting pieces, king safety, or structural preconditions needed to make it work are absent. The opponent consistently refutes not by accepting the pawn's challenge but by exploiting the tempo loss or newly created weaknesses elsewhere.

36.label: A knight move that appears active or forcing but allows the opponent to gain tempo by attacking the relocated knight immediately.
36.description: In every position, a knight is moved to an apparently active, centralized, or tactically motivated square, but the destination square is immediately challenged by the opponent's next move—forcing the knight to retreat or concede material. The player believed the knight move was safe or even aggressive, but failed to see that the new square was vulnerable to a pawn push, piece development with tempo, or direct attack that unraveled their position. The core error is not simply moving the knight, but moving it to a square where the opponent gains a free developing or attacking move, effectively losing a full tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.

37.label: Player makes a 'logical' move pursuing their own plan while completely overlooking an immediate tactical or strategic threat already present on the board.
37.description: In every position, the player focuses on executing their intended idea — developing a piece, advancing a pawn, centralizing a queen — without first asking 'what does my opponent threaten?' The refutation in each case is a direct, often forcing response that exploits something the player's move failed to address or actively worsened. The unifying coaching lesson is the habit of candidate-move thinking: before playing your plan, always check if your opponent has an immediate threat you must answer first.

38.label: Mishandling critical moments in endgames dominated by passed pawns or pawn races.
38.description: Every position involves a late-game scenario where passed pawns, pawn promotion races, or king-and-pawn endgame technique is the central strategic theme. The blunders consistently involve either neglecting a passed pawn's advancement, misplacing a piece that should contest or escort a passed pawn, or losing tempo in positions where pawn promotion timing is decisive. The feature fires on endgame moves where the player fails to correctly prioritize passed pawn dynamics — whether by moving away from the critical file, allowing the opponent's passer to advance freely, or choosing an active-looking move that abandons pawn race arithmetic.

39.label: The queen relocates to a square where it immediately becomes a target, allowing the opponent to gain tempo or material through direct attack.
39.description: In every position, the player moves their queen to what appears to be an active or safe square, but the new square exposes the queen to immediate attack — by a bishop, knight, pawn fork, or discovered attack — forcing it to move again or resulting in material loss. The common failure is not calculating how the opponent can gain a tempo or decisive advantage by simply attacking the misplaced queen on its new square. This pattern unifies blunders across all tactical motifs: the queen's relocation is the root cause regardless of whether the refutation is a fork, pin, discovered attack, or hanging piece.

40.label: A pawn advances to grab space or create threats but loses tempo and ignores a stronger opponent response.
40.description: In every position, the player pushes a pawn forward with an apparent strategic or tactical purpose — gaining space, fixing weaknesses, or creating threats — but the advance either ignores an immediate tactical refutation or surrenders the initiative by allowing the opponent to respond with a stronger move elsewhere. The pawn move is self-defeating: it either weakens the king's defenses (enabling sacrifices like Bxh2+), surrenders a tempo that lets the opponent seize a dominant outpost or activate a piece, or fixes the pawn structure in a way that creates new static weaknesses rather than solving problems. The unifying coaching lesson is that pawn advances cannot be taken back, so each such move must be evaluated not just for what it threatens but for what stronger reply it enables.

41.label: Voluntarily exchanging or trading rooks that eliminates the player's own winning advantage or creates a decisive tactical vulnerability.
41.description: In every position, the blundering player initiates or accepts a rook trade/simplification on an open file, believing the exchange is neutral or favorable, but the recapture activates the opponent's pieces, opens critical lines, or removes the key defensive or attacking rook at exactly the wrong moment. The common thread is not the tactical motif of what follows, but the decision to simplify with a rook move that hands the opponent a concrete advantage — whether through recapture improving a piece, exposing a king, or surrendering a dominant file. The feature fires on positions where a player's rook move to exchange or trade rooks is the root cause of squandering an existing advantage.

42.label: A knight moves to an apparently powerful central or attacking square but loses time when the opponent simply responds with a developing or defensive move that ignores or refutes the threat.
42.description: In every position, a knight is moved to what looks like a dominant outpost (e5, d5, g5, d4, e4, etc.) with the intention of centralizing aggressively or creating threats. However, the opponent has a calm, often simple response — retreating a piece, developing with tempo, or exploiting the square the knight just vacated — that either ignores the threat entirely or turns the tables. The unifying pattern is that the knight leap appears active but actually concedes the initiative, wastes a tempo, or leaves key squares undefended, resulting in a significant material or positional loss.

43.label: A pawn advances aggressively but the square or pawn it moves to is immediately capturable, losing material or fatally weakening the position.
43.description: In every case, a player pushes a pawn one square forward with an ostensibly purposeful intention (central break, passed pawn advance, space gain, or promotion threat), but the pawn is either undefended and immediately captured for free, or its advance removes a key defender causing a cascade of material loss. The unifying pattern is that the pawn move looks purposeful or even thematic but ignores the simple tactical reality that the pawn can be taken at once with no adequate compensation.

44.label: A king move that either walks into immediate checkmate or drastically worsens the king's safety by stepping onto a square where it becomes fatally exposed.
44.description: In every position, the side to move plays a king move intended to escape pressure, centralize, or find safety — but instead the king steps onto a square where it is immediately checkmated or enters a forced mate sequence within a few moves. The unifying pattern is not a specific tactical motif but the king's self-destruction through voluntary movement: the king walks away from a bad-but-survivable position directly into a geometrically fatal square where attacking pieces converge. The feature captures the moment a king move transforms a defensible (if losing) position into an immediate or near-immediate forced mate.

45.label: A pawn advance made to chase or challenge an enemy piece creates a new tactical or structural weakness that is immediately exploited.
45.description: In every position, the blundering player pushes a pawn to attack, restrict, or drive away an opponent's piece — but the pawn move weakens a square, removes a key defender, or opens a diagonal/file that the opponent immediately exploits with a stronger counter. The intent is defensive or reactive (chase the bishop, challenge the knight, block the diagonal), but the pawn's departure from its original square creates a vulnerability worse than the problem it was trying to solve. This is the classic 'solving one problem while creating a bigger one' pattern seen in all skill levels.

46.label: A piece move that creates or exposes a critical weakness by vacating its current square or opening a line.
46.description: In every case, the blundering move relocates a piece that was performing a vital defensive or positional duty, and the act of moving it away creates an immediately exploitable hole — whether that is an undefended piece, an exposed king, a newly opened diagonal, or a square the piece was guarding. The refutation in each case directly punishes the vacancy left behind rather than the piece's new destination. The unifying coaching lesson is: before moving any piece, verify what it is currently doing and what breaks the moment it leaves.

47.label: Moves flagged as blunders that are actually the engine's top choice with zero centipawn loss.
47.description: Every single position in this set involves a move that was incorrectly labeled as a blunder by the data pipeline, yet each move is objectively the best available with 0 centipawn loss and often the only good move. The SAE feature appears to detect a systematic mislabeling artifact: winning moves in already-decided positions being flagged as errors, likely because the evaluation difference between a forced mate and a 'merely winning' continuation appears large in raw centipawn terms. The unifying coaching pattern is not a tactical mistake but a data quality issue — the feature activates on best moves that were falsely classified as blunders.

48.label: A king move that appears safe or logical but immediately exposes the king to a decisive tactical blow.
48.description: In every position, the player moves their king to a square that seems reasonable—centralizing, escaping checks, or tucking away—but the new square creates or reveals a specific tactical vulnerability: a check, fork, skewer, discovered attack, or back-rank weakness. The opponent then immediately exploits the king's new position with a forcing sequence that either mates or wins decisive material. The unifying theme is not passive king safety but the failure to calculate how the king's destination square enables a concrete enemy tactic.

49.label: Player makes an active pawn or piece move that neglects an immediate, stronger enemy response that exploits the resulting weaknesses or undefended pieces.
49.description: In every position, the blundering side makes what appears to be a purposeful aggressive or constructive move (typically a pawn advance or piece activation) without accounting for the opponent's most forcing reply, which either wins material, exploits a newly created weakness, or launches a decisive counterattack. The common coaching failure is that the player acts as if their plan executes in a vacuum, ignoring that the opponent gets to respond immediately — often with a move that is stronger precisely because of what the blunder just changed. Each blunder creates a 'tempo gift': the opponent's refutation gains time and advantage directly from the move just played.

50.label: Playing a natural developing move that ignores an immediate tactical or strategic crisis requiring urgent attention.
50.description: In every case, the player chooses a textbook developing move (Nf3, Nc3, Nf6, Nc6, Nd7, Ne2, etc.) that would be perfectly correct in a quiet position, but the position has already reached a critical moment where development must be delayed to handle a concrete threat, capture a hanging piece, or exploit a fleeting tactical opportunity. The unifying pattern is the conflict between automatic 'good principles' play and the discipline to recognize when the position demands a non-routine, forcing response instead. The feature fires on positions where following general opening principles is itself the blunder.

51.label: A pawn move played with a different strategic intent simultaneously allows an enemy piece to be captured for free.
51.description: In every case, the player makes a pawn advance aimed at a specific goal (space gain, pawn storm, prophylaxis, attacking a piece) while completely overlooking that a friendly piece elsewhere on the board is undefended and immediately capturable. The pawn move wastes a tempo on an irrelevant objective, and the opponent simply takes the hanging piece, winning material outright. The feature detects the pattern of a purposeful-looking pawn move that ignores a pre-existing or newly created loose piece vulnerability.

52.label: A piece moves to an apparently active or central square but abandons a critical defensive duty or misses the tempo needed to survive.
52.description: In every position, the player relocates a rook, queen, or other piece to what looks like an aggressive or centralizing square, but the move either neglects a key defensive responsibility, hands the opponent a decisive tempo, or allows an immediate tactical refutation that the previous square would have prevented. The common coaching lesson is that 'active-looking' moves must be checked for what they stop guarding or what counterplay they allow before being played. The feature fires when a piece move prioritizes apparent activity over concrete calculation of the opponent's immediate threats.

53.label: A piece moves away from a key defensive or controlling square, immediately creating a vulnerability that the opponent exploits.
53.description: In every position, the blundering side moves a piece to a seemingly logical or developing square, but in doing so abandons a critical defensive duty — vacating a key square, diagonal, or file that the opponent immediately exploits. The new piece placement does not create compensating threats, so the opponent simply punishes the newly created hole, pin, fork opportunity, or undefended piece. The unifying pattern is not the specific tactic used to punish, but rather the coach's lesson: before relocating a piece, verify what it was guarding or controlling, because voluntary removal of a defender or controller is the root cause of the collapse.

54.label: A piece leaps to an apparently dominant central square but is immediately captured or exploited because the square is not adequately defended or the move creates new tactical vulnerabilities.
54.description: In every position, the blundering side plays a knight (or occasionally bishop) to an aggressive-looking central square — most commonly d5 or e4/e5 — believing they are seizing control or creating threats. However, the piece is either immediately captured with gain of tempo, triggers a fork or discovered attack, or vacates a square that the opponent immediately exploits. The unifying coaching lesson is: before occupying an 'outpost,' verify the piece is actually safe there and that moving it doesn't create new weaknesses elsewhere.

55.label: Playing a natural-looking knight development move while ignoring an urgent tactical or positional threat that punishes the tempo loss.
55.description: In every position, the blundering side plays a knight to a seemingly logical, 'good' square (centralization, development, activation) as if the position were quiet, while the opponent has or immediately creates a concrete threat that the knight move does nothing to address. The move is not objectively bad in a vacuum — it looks principled — but it wastes the one tempo needed to deal with a king attack, a hanging piece, a fork, or a decisive pawn break. The unifying coaching lesson is: before making any 'improving' knight move, verify there is no forcing continuation your opponent can unleash this very move.

56.label: Player initiates an exchange or simplification that resolves tactical tension but transitions into a structurally or materially lost endgame.
56.description: In every case, the blundering side makes a move that appears to resolve immediate threats or win material by forcing trades, but the resulting simplified position (pawn ending, rook ending, or queen-less middlegame) is objectively lost due to factors like passed pawns, king activity, or piece coordination that were obscured by the pre-trade complexity. The common coaching lesson is that simplification is not inherently safe — the player must evaluate the resulting endgame, not just the immediate exchange. The feature fires when a player trades into or voluntarily simplifies toward an ending without accurately assessing the static factors that will dominate once the dynamic tension is removed.

57.label: A rook move activates or repositions the rook but fatally abandons a square or piece it was uniquely defending.
57.description: In every position, the player moves a rook away from a critical defensive post to pursue an active or logical-seeming goal elsewhere. The rook's departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability — an undefended piece, an unguarded back rank, or an exposed pawn — that the opponent exploits directly on the next move. The unifying pattern is not what the rook does on its new square, but what it stops doing on its old one.

58.label: Player executes a discovered check or attack but the moving piece lands on a inferior square, allowing the opponent to sidestep or counterattack effectively.
58.description: In every position, the player correctly identifies a discovered check or discovered attack mechanism but chooses the wrong destination square for the moving piece—either landing it on a vulnerable square, missing a stronger landing square, or giving the opponent a simple escape or interposition. The refutation is consistently a calm king step, queen interposition, or counter-tactic that exploits the poorly placed piece, turning a winning or equal position into a loss. The unifying error is not failing to see the discovered attack concept, but misjudging which square the triggering piece should occupy.

59.label: A quiet, non-threatening pawn move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit a hanging piece/tactical opportunity.
59.description: In every position, the losing side plays a small, ostensibly 'safe' pawn move (a3, a6, h3, c3, f3, b5, g6, etc.) intended to solidify, prophylax, or prepare something, when the position demanded an immediate active response. The opponent then uses the gifted tempo to activate a key piece, launch a decisive attack, or execute a tactic that was only possible because the 'helpful' pawn move did nothing to address the real threat. The unifying pattern is: a positionally-motivated but strategically passive pawn nudge in a position where urgency required concrete action.

60.label: A bishop moves to an active or greedy square but vacates a key defensive post, creating immediate tactical or strategic problems.
60.description: In every case, a bishop moves away from its current square to capture material, deliver check, or target an enemy piece — but the departure square was more important than the destination. The opponent immediately exploits either the newly undefended piece/pawn the bishop was protecting, the weakened diagonal or color complex left behind, or the bishop itself becomes trapped or overextended on its new square. The common coaching lesson is: before moving a bishop aggressively, verify what it was guarding and whether it can safely return.

61.label: Detects single-pawn prophylactic or preparatory moves (luft, fianchetto setup) that lose a critical tempo and allow immediate punishment.
61.description: In every position, the blundering player makes a one-pawn move intended as preparation — either a luft escape square (h3, h6, a3, b6) or a fianchetto setup (g3, g6, b3) — rather than addressing the board's most urgent demand. Because the move contributes nothing concrete to the position and wastes a full tempo, the opponent immediately exploits the resulting tactical or positional gap: hanging pieces go uncaptured, back ranks collapse, forks land, or passed pawns advance unopposed. The unifying pattern is the fatal mismatch between the move's modest local intent and the position's urgent global needs.

62.label: A piece moves to an ostensibly active or logical square while completely failing to address an existing or newly created tactical vulnerability.
62.description: In every position, the player executes a move with a plausible strategic or tactical intention (centralizing a piece, developing, attacking) but the chosen piece vacates a key defensive square, opens a line, or simply ignores an imminent forcing threat — allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the resulting weakness with a check, fork, capture, or mating sequence. The move 'looks right' in isolation but is disconnected from the actual urgency of the position, leaving a critical problem unresolved or newly exposed.

63.label: A rook is ambitiously lifted or repositioned along a rank or file, but the move creates immediate tactical or strategic vulnerabilities that the opponent exploits decisively.
63.description: In every position, a player moves a rook to an 'active' square—typically a lift along the third, fourth, fifth, or sixth rank, or a swing to an open file—with the intent of generating pressure or doubling rooks. However, the rook move either abandons a critical defensive duty (back rank, guarding a piece, blocking a diagonal) or lands on a square where it becomes a target, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit forks, hanging pieces, back-rank weaknesses, or discovered attacks. The unifying coaching lesson is that rook activity must be checked against the tactical consequences of vacating the original square and the safety of the new square before executing the lift.

64.label: Capturing a pawn or resolving tension creates a fatal vulnerability that the opponent immediately exploits.
64.description: In every position, the blundering side captures a pawn or releases central/pawn tension in a way that appears to gain material or simplify, but the capture itself opens a file, diagonal, or rank, removes a key defender, or abandons a critical square that allows the opponent to launch a decisive attack. The player prioritizes the immediate material or structural gain without recognizing that the act of capturing transforms the position in a way that enables a forcing refutation—check, mate threat, or winning tactical shot—that did not exist before the capture. The unifying coaching lesson is: before capturing, ask what the position looks like after the capture, not just whether the piece being taken is defended.

65.label: A knight move that undefends a piece or square, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness.
65.description: In every position, the blundering side moves a knight to what appears to be a more active or safer square, but in doing so removes it from a critical defensive duty — leaving a pawn, piece, or key square completely unprotected. The opponent immediately capitalizes on the abandoned defense, whether by capturing the now-hanging piece, delivering checkmate through the vacated square, or winning material via fork or discovered attack. The common coaching lesson is: before moving a knight, always verify what it was defending on its current square.

66.label: A move relocates a piece but abandons a critical square or line, immediately creating a tactical weakness the opponent exploits.
66.description: In every position, the blundering player moves a piece to what appears to be an active or safe square, but the act of leaving the original square opens a diagonal, file, rank, or undefended square that the opponent immediately exploits — via check, fork, discovered attack, or material win. The unifying pattern is not the tactical motif itself but the root cause: the moved piece was the sole guardian of a vulnerability, and its departure creates an instant, decisive refutation. This is the 'loose piece / abandoned square' pattern where the player focuses on the destination of their piece while ignoring what the origin square was defending.

67.label: A pawn advance that appears purposeful but fatally weakens a key square, file, or defensive structure.
67.description: In every position, the blunder is a pawn move that the player intended to gain space, attack a piece, or consolidate, but which instead opened a critical line, vacated a key defensive square, or created an irreparable weakness that the opponent immediately exploits. The pawn move is the root cause: it cannot be undone, and it directly enables the refutation by removing or displacing the very pawn that was doing defensive or structural work. Unlike tactical piece blunders, these are pawn advances that look constructive but permanently compromise the position.

68.label: A knight moves to an apparently powerful square but is immediately captured or tactically refuted because it lacks sufficient protection.
68.description: In every position, a knight is aggressively deployed to what appears to be a dominant outpost, fork, or attacking square, but the move fails because the knight can simply be captured or the opponent has an immediate tactical resource that the player missed while focusing on the knight's apparent threats. The common coaching lesson is that before placing a knight on an 'active' square, the player must verify it is adequately defended and that no immediate refutation (capture, counter-threat, or deflection) exists. The feature captures the cognitive pattern of being seduced by a knight's visual dominance on a square while ignoring basic piece safety.

69.label: Premature bishop or knight sacrifice on king-zone squares (f2, f7, h2, h7) that lacks sufficient follow-up compensation.
69.description: In every position, the player sacrifices a piece on a square adjacent to or defended solely by the enemy king (f7, f2, h2, or h7), typically delivering check and hoping to exploit king exposure. The opponent simply captures the sacrificing piece and emerges a full minor piece ahead, because the attacker lacks the necessary supporting pieces, open lines, or tactical continuations to generate real threats. The unifying error is pattern-matching to famous sacrificial motifs (Greek Gift, Fried Liver) without verifying that the concrete follow-up compensation actually exists.

70.label: A seemingly purposeful or aggressive move overlooks an immediate tactical refutation that punishes the piece's new square or the weakness it creates.
70.description: In every position, the player makes a move with clear strategic or aggressive intent—developing a piece, activating a queen, attacking an enemy piece, or delivering check—but fails to calculate that the move itself creates or leaves a concrete tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, undefended square, exposed king, or abandoned defender) that the opponent immediately exploits. The blunder is not passive or positional drift but rather an 'active' move whose very activity blinds the player to the tactical consequences of leaving the previous position. The unifying pattern is the gap between intent (do something purposeful) and calculation (verify the new position is tactically safe).

71.label: Blunders where the strategic plan to double rooks on a file or rank ignores immediate tactical refutations.
71.description: In every position, the player executes the classic doubling-rooks maneuver (on a file, rank, or the 7th) as a strategic plan, but the tempo spent repositioning the rook creates or exposes a tactical vulnerability the opponent immediately exploits. The common failure is prioritizing a long-term positional idea over short-term tactical alertness — the doubled rooks never get to exert their intended pressure because the position collapses first. This feature detects the specific moment when 'doubling rooks' is the stated intent of a move that turns out to be a blunder.

72.label: Moving the queen to an apparently active central or connecting square that immediately becomes a target or abandons a critical defensive duty.
72.description: In every position, the player moves their queen to what looks like an improved square — centralizing, connecting rooks, or adding pressure — but the queen immediately becomes exposed to tempo-gaining attacks (knight forks, rook attacks, pawn advances) or vacates a square that was essential for defense, allowing decisive tactical shots. The common coaching lesson is that queen activity must be evaluated not just by the queen's new power, but by what attacks it invites and what it stops guarding.

73.label: A rook (or major piece) is moved to an undefended square where it is immediately captured for free.
73.description: In every position, the blundering player moves a rook (occasionally a queen) to an active-looking square — typically an open file, rank invasion, or checking square — without noticing that the piece can be immediately captured by an opponent's piece with no compensation. The intent is always plausible (7th rank invasion, check, centralization, back-rank pressure), but the moved piece lands on a square directly attacked and completely undefended, resulting in losing an entire major piece for nothing. The unifying coaching lesson is: before any rook move, verify the destination square is not immediately capturable.

74.label: Captures that allow the opponent to recapture with strong piece activation, turning a seemingly profitable exchange into a positional or tactical disaster.
74.description: In every position, the blundering player initiates a capture expecting to win material or remove a piece, but the opponent's recapture lands a piece (queen, rook, or knight) on a powerful, centralized square with tempo and activity. The player failed to evaluate the recapturing piece's resulting strength — the exchange gifted the opponent a dominant piece placement that swung the evaluation by 200-600 centipawns. The unifying coaching lesson is: before capturing, always ask 'how does my opponent recapture, and how strong will that piece be?'

75.label: King activation and centralization moves in pure pawn endgames
75.description: Every position features a king move aimed at centralizing or advancing toward pawns in a late-stage endgame with few or no pieces remaining. The feature fires on king step moves that are part of a king march plan — escorting passed pawns, opposing the enemy king, or racing to capture pawns — regardless of whether the move is correct or erroneous. The unifying element is not the quality of the move but the structural context: a pawn endgame where king activity and optimal routing are the dominant strategic theme.

76.label: Moves that reposition a rook (or major piece) to a seemingly logical square while fatally neglecting an existing tactical or structural vulnerability.
76.description: In every case, the player makes a plausible-looking rook (or occasionally other piece) maneuver aimed at doubling on a file, centralizing, or defending — but the move either blocks a critical defensive line, abandons a key square, or consumes a tempo that allows the opponent to exploit an already-present weakness. The common thread is not the piece type per se, but that the repositioning move fails because it ignores an immediate tactical refutation (hanging piece, fork, king exposure, trapped piece) that the player could not afford to overlook. The feature appears to detect positions where a 'logical-looking' rearrangement move is punished by a forcing response that was already latent in the position.

77.label: A bishop move that looks active or safe but abandons a critical defensive or tactical duty, immediately allowing a devastating refutation.
77.description: In every case, the player moves a bishop to what appears to be an active, safe, or consolidating square, but the relocation removes the bishop from a square where it was performing an essential function—defending the king, controlling a key diagonal, guarding a piece, or blockading a passed pawn. The opponent immediately exploits the vacated square or the newly exposed weakness, whether through a fork, skewer, back-rank tactic, hanging piece, or direct king attack. The feature fires on bishop moves where the apparent activity of the destination square masks the critical duty being abandoned at the origin square.

78.label: Detects positions where a passed pawn is on the verge of promotion or actively promoting to a queen.
78.description: Every position features a passed pawn advancing to the seventh rank, reaching the eighth rank, or actually promoting to a queen — the defining moment of pawn promotion sequences. The feature fires strongly regardless of whether the promotion move is a blunder, an inaccuracy, or the objectively best move, indicating it tracks the structural and tactical context of imminent queening rather than move quality. The unifying coaching concept is recognizing and executing passed pawn promotion, the single most decisive operation in king-and-pawn endgames.

79.label: A capture that removes one problem but immediately creates a worse vulnerability elsewhere.
79.description: In every position, the player executes a seemingly logical capture — taking a piece, pawn, or intruder — but the act of capturing either vacates a critical defensive square, opens a line, displaces the king, or surrenders tempo in a way that hands the opponent a devastating follow-up. The blunder is not that the captured piece was worthless, but that the capture itself was the mistake: the opponent's best reply exploits the new weakness created by the capture move, not the position before it. The unifying lesson is that before taking, the player must ask 'what does my opponent get after I capture?' rather than only 'what do I gain?'

80.label: A pawn capture that gains material or relieves tension while fatally weakening the king's shelter or removing a critical defensive pawn.
80.description: In every position, the blunderer makes a pawn capture that appears to win material, relieve pressure, or simplify the position, but the act of capturing removes a pawn that was silently performing a critical defensive function — guarding the king, blocking an open file, or preventing a tactical leap. The refutation immediately exploits the newly created hole, open file, or undefended piece that the capture exposed. The unifying lesson is that pawn captures must be evaluated not just for what they gain but for what defensive duty the capturing pawn abandons.

81.label: Rook moves to an inactive or wrong square, allowing the opposing king to march forward decisively.
81.description: In every position, a rook is repositioned to a square that looks active or defensive but fails to control the critical files, ranks, or entry squares needed to stop the opponent's winning plan. The refutation in nearly all cases involves the enemy king simply stepping forward or a passed pawn advancing, because the rook no longer cuts off the king or blockades the pawn. The unifying coaching lesson is that rook activity must be measured by whether it restrains the opponent's king or passed pawn, not by superficial targets like pawns or checks.

82.label: Player captures an apparently free or valuable piece while ignoring a decisive tactical consequence that the capture enables.
82.description: In every position, the player executes what looks like a straightforward material gain — capturing a hanging piece, rook, or pawn — without recognizing that the act of capturing either removes a critical defensive pawn/piece, opens a file or diagonal, or shifts focus away from an immediate forced sequence that either mates or wins far more decisively. The unifying error is the tunnel-vision pursuit of the visible material reward while neglecting the positional or tactical transformation the capture itself creates. This is the classic 'winning a piece but losing the game' pattern, where the capture is the blunder regardless of how tempting the target appears.

83.label: Moving the queen to a new square that immediately becomes a target or abandons a critical defensive/offensive duty.
83.description: In every case, the player repositioned their queen believing the new square was active or safe, but the move either placed the queen on a square where it could be attacked with tempo, abandoned a piece or pawn it was defending, or vacated a square that was crucial for the position's integrity. The opponent could immediately exploit the queen's new placement — whether by attacking it directly, winning undefended material, or launching a decisive tactic the queen's departure enabled. The unifying theme is that queen moves which appear to improve or consolidate actually hand the initiative to the opponent by creating a new weakness or losing a tempo.

84.label: A piece captures what appears to be free material but lands undefended and is immediately recaptured at a net loss.
84.description: In every position, the blundering player executes a capture — pawn, piece, or pawn-grab — placing their own piece on a square where it has no protection and can be immediately taken back by the opponent, losing material outright. The player correctly identified a target but fatally miscounted the defenders, failing to verify that the landing square was safe after the capture. This is the classic 'hanging piece after capture' pattern: the attacker wins the target but donates their own piece in return.

85.label: A piece captures aggressively but leaves another piece or pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to recapture or take the newly exposed target for free.
85.description: In every case, the blundering side makes a capture (often motivated by pawn-grabbing, attacking the king, or forcing checks) that either removes a defender or displaces a piece, immediately leaving a different piece, pawn, or key square undefended. The opponent then simply takes the newly hanging material or delivers an immediate decisive blow that the blunderer failed to see was possible after their capture. The unifying thread is not the specific tactic used to punish but the structural oversight: the capture itself creates or reveals an undefended target that the opponent exploits immediately.

86.label: A pawn capture or advance unguards a piece or opens a file/diagonal that is immediately exploited by the opponent.
86.description: In every case, the blundering side moves a pawn (usually a capture) that clears a rank, file, or diagonal which was previously blocked or protected by that pawn, leaving a piece — queen, rook, or king — suddenly exposed and vulnerable to immediate tactical punishment. The player focused on the material or positional gain of the pawn move while completely missing that the pawn itself was serving as a critical shield or blocker. The refutation in each case directly exploits the newly opened line or newly undefended piece that the pawn departure revealed.

87.label: Bishop aggressively leaves its post to attack or sacrifice, creating tactical vulnerabilities that the opponent immediately exploits.
87.description: In every position, a bishop makes an ambitious attacking or 'active' move — sacrificing on f7/h7/h6/h2/h3, capturing a defended piece, or relocating to an aggressive square — without sufficient preparation or support. The opponent refutes the bishop's adventure by either simply accepting free material, exploiting the square the bishop abandoned, or ignoring the threat entirely and striking elsewhere. The unifying coaching lesson is that bishop attacks must be carefully calculated before execution; an unsupported bishop sortie typically loses material or concedes a decisive positional advantage.

88.label: Capturing an apparently free pawn while ignoring a decisive tactical or positional threat.
88.description: In every position, the blundering player captured what appeared to be an undefended or easily won pawn, redirecting their piece away from a critical defensive or offensive duty. This pawn capture either removed a piece from a key defensive square, allowed a devastating counter-attack (fork, checkmate, passed pawn promotion), or wasted the tempo needed to execute a winning plan. The common coaching lesson is: before grabbing a 'free' pawn, verify there is no immediate tactical refutation enabled by the piece's new position.

89.label: Moving a knight to an apparently better square that ignores an immediate tactical or strategic threat elsewhere on the board.
89.description: In every position, the player moves a knight to what looks like a more active, central, or logical square, but the relocation either abandons a defensive duty, leaves a piece or pawn undefended, or allows the opponent an immediate forcing reply that the knight's presence had previously prevented. The unifying pattern is not the motif of the refutation (which varies: forks, hanging pieces, passed pawns, king safety) but the trigger: a knight move that prioritizes repositioning over concrete threats, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness before the knight can prove its worth on its new square.

90.label: Aggressively advancing a pawn loses material, tempo, or creates fatal weaknesses the opponent immediately exploits.
90.description: In every case, the blundering side pushes a pawn forward with an ambitious goal (creating a passed pawn, gaining space, or attacking) but the advance either removes a key defender, opens a diagonal or file for the opponent, or wastes a critical tempo that allows the opponent to strike first. The pawn move looks purposeful but concretely backfires because the opponent has an immediate tactical or positional response that the advancing player failed to anticipate. The unifying coaching lesson is: before advancing a pawn, verify it does not lose a defender, open lines against your own king, or squander the initiative.

91.label: A knight move activates or repositions the piece while leaving another piece or square undefended, allowing immediate material capture.
91.description: In every position, a knight is moved with an apparent purpose (development, forking, winning material, or regrouping), but the move abandons the defense of a piece elsewhere on the board that was relying on the knight. The opponent responds not by addressing the knight's threat but by simply capturing the now-unprotected piece, winning material immediately. The coaching lesson is: before moving a knight, verify what it is currently defending, because knights are the easiest piece to overlook as defenders.

92.label: A knight relocation that looks natural or safe but immediately creates a tactical or structural liability the opponent exploits decisively.
92.description: In every position, the player moves a knight to what appears to be a centralizing, retreating, or repositioning square, but the move either abandons a key defensive duty, steps onto a square where it is immediately attacked or trapped, or removes a piece that was indirectly holding the position together. The opponent then exploits the resulting weakness—often a fork, a hanging piece elsewhere, a pawn attack on the knight, or an unguarded diagonal/square—with a forcing reply that wins material or seizes a decisive advantage.

93.label: A rook move that vacates a key defensive or controlling square, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
93.description: In every position, a rook is relocated to what appears to be an active or logical square, but the departure square was performing a critical defensive function — guarding the back rank, controlling an open file, supporting a key pawn, or sheltering the king. The refutations consistently exploit the newly vacated square or line rather than attacking the rook's new position. The coaching lesson is: before moving a rook, verify what it is currently doing, not just where it is going.

94.label: Moving the a-rook (or h-rook) to a central file loses critical tempo that the opponent exploits immediately.
94.description: In virtually every position, the player moves a rook from a corner file (a1, a8, h1, h8) to a central open file (d, e, or f) as a natural-looking developing or file-contesting move. However, the tempo spent on this rook centralization allows the opponent to execute a tactic — fork, discovered attack, bishop attack on the queen, king safety resolution, or piece trap — that was only possible because the rook move failed to address the position's most urgent demands. The feature captures the pattern of 'routine rook activation' that ignores an immediate tactical or positional threat requiring a different priority.

95.label: Moving a piece to an ostensibly active square that immediately creates a new, fatal weakness or leaves another piece/square undefended.
95.description: In every case, the player moves a piece with a plausible-looking purpose (developing a bishop, pushing a pawn for space, activating a rook) but the destination square either abandons a critical defensive duty, exposes the king, or leaves another piece hanging. The move is not obviously losing on its face — it has a coherent intent — but it creates an immediate, concrete tactical or structural concession the opponent can exploit at once. The unifying coaching lesson is: before relocating a piece, verify what it was previously guarding and whether the new square creates weaknesses that outweigh the gains.

96.label: Queen relocates to an 'active' square while ignoring an immediate tactical or safety refutation enabled by the new queen position.
96.description: In every case, the player moves their queen to what appears to be a centralizing, activating, or pressure-generating square, but the new queen position either abandons a critical defensive duty, exposes the king to a check or mating attack, or leaves a piece/pawn undefended that the queen previously covered. The refutation is consistently direct and forcing—a check, a fork, a capture, or a mate threat—that would not have existed had the queen stayed put or chosen a safer route. The feature captures the pattern of queen activity that prioritizes aggression or centralization over concrete calculation of what the queen's departure allows.

97.label: Playing a move that fails to address an immediate tactical or positional threat, allowing the opponent to execute a powerful response.
97.description: In every position, the player makes a plausible-looking move (development, prophylaxis, king safety, pawn advance) that simply ignores a concrete threat or opportunity available to the opponent. The move played has some local logic but fails to account for what the opponent can do immediately in response — a fork, a hanging piece, a king attack, or a tempo-winning sequence. The unifying coaching lesson is: before playing your move, ask 'what can my opponent do next?' — these blunders all share the failure to perform that check.

98.label: Incorrectly trading pieces to simplify into a worse or losing position
98.description: In every position, the player initiates or accepts a piece exchange (most often a queen trade) believing simplification will favor them, but the recapture or resulting simplified position turns out to benefit the opponent decisively. The unifying error is a faulty assessment that 'trading off pieces will help me' when in fact the opponent's recapture activates a piece, opens a file, creates a passed pawn, or removes the defender needed to hold the position. The feature detects the cognitive pattern of seeking relief through exchanges without accurately calculating the post-trade dynamics.

99.label: Premature or misdirected pawn advances that ignore the opponent's strongest tactical or positional response.
99.description: In every position, the blundering side pushes a pawn (or captures with a pawn) believing it gains space, wins material, or creates threats, but fatally ignores what the opponent can do in reply—whether a discovered attack, a newly opened file against the king, a fork, or simply a stronger counterthrust. The pawn move typically either wastes a critical tempo, opens lines against one's own king, or surrenders a key structural or tactical resource that the opponent immediately exploits. The unifying coaching lesson is: before pushing a pawn, ask what your opponent's best reply is, because pawn moves cannot be taken back.

100.label: King moves into exposed squares that allow immediate tactical exploitation by the opponent
100.description: In every position, the side to move relocates their king to a square that appears safe or purposeful (centralizing, escaping checks, tucking away) but instead places the king on an unguarded diagonal, file, or rank that the opponent immediately exploits with checks, forks, skewers, or checkmate. The unifying pattern is a king move that ignores or misjudges how the new square intersects with opponent piece lines, converting a survivable position into a decisive loss. The feature fires on king moves where the king's destination is tactically vulnerable to forcing sequences the player failed to calculate.

101.label: Developing a bishop to an active-looking square that immediately gets exploited by a fork, pin, or tempo-gaining attack.
101.description: In every position, a player moves a bishop off its starting square to what appears to be an active developing square, but the new square is immediately vulnerable to a tactical refutation — most commonly a pawn fork, knight fork, or queen attack that hits the bishop while also threatening something else. The bishop development is not wrong in principle but wrong in timing or square selection, because the opponent can immediately punish the specific square chosen with a forcing move that wins material or a decisive tempo advantage.

102.label: A king move that misplaces the king, either stepping into tactical danger or abandoning a critical defensive or offensive post.
102.description: In every position, the blunder is a king move that looks plausible—centralizing, fleeing checks, or seeking shelter—but places the king on a square where it becomes a tactical liability or loses a crucial tempo. The misplaced king either steps into a fork, exposes itself to a rook check or back-rank mate, abandons an undefended pawn, or simply wastes a critical move in a race where every tempo counts. The unifying coaching lesson is that king moves in endgames and critical middlegame transitions must be evaluated not just for where the king is going, but for what it leaves behind and what threats the new square invites.

103.label: Detects prophylactic king sidesteps that waste a critical tempo and allow the opponent to seize initiative or exploit hanging material.
103.description: In every position, the player moves their king one square to a seemingly safer square (Kh1, Ka2, Kh7, Kb8, etc.) under the mistaken belief they are preventing a future threat or improving king safety. However, the king move is not forced, accomplishes nothing concrete, and hands the opponent a free tempo to capture hanging pieces, advance pawns with tempo, or unleash decisive combinations. The unifying coaching lesson is: do not make passive king moves when the position demands active piece play — a wasted king move in a critical moment is almost always a losing concession.

104.label: A bishop relocation that neglects a critical defensive or tactical duty, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated square or diagonal.
104.description: In every position, a bishop moves to what appears to be a more active or logical square, but in doing so it abandons a key defensive responsibility — whether guarding a square, controlling a diagonal, or sheltering the king. The opponent immediately punishes this by forking, checking, skewering, or advancing a passer through the newly weakened area. The unifying pattern is not the specific tactic used against it, but the root cause: a bishop move that looks constructive but creates an exploitable hole the moment it leaves its prior post.

105.label: A knight moves away from a square or piece it was defending, immediately creating a tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits.
105.description: In every position, a knight relocates to what appears to be a more active or useful square, but in doing so it abandons a critical defensive or structural duty — unguarding a piece, opening a diagonal, or leaving a square undefended. The opponent then immediately exploits the vacated square or newly unprotected piece, typically winning material or delivering checkmate. The feature captures the recurring pattern where the knight's departure, not its destination, is the source of the blunder.

106.label: Moving the rook to an active-looking but wrong square while missing the opponent's most forcing response
106.description: In every position, the player relocates their rook to what appears to be an aggressive or logical square (seventh rank, open file, attacking a pawn) but in doing so abandons a critical defensive or offensive duty, allowing the opponent to immediately execute a stronger plan — a fork, a passed pawn advance, a king march, or a back-rank tactic. The unifying pattern is a rook move that looks purposeful but is one tempo too slow or one square off, giving the opponent exactly the tempo needed to seize decisive control. The feature captures the recurring coaching lesson: before moving your rook, check whether the opponent has an immediate forcing reply that your rook's new square fails to address.

107.label: Advancing a passer prematurely when another move wins immediately or maintains the advantage.
